name: Joel
sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew Masoretic Text as given in the Westminster Leningrad Codex (Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible edition), with the Septuagint (Old Greek) consulted. The date of Joel is uncertain; the book names no king, and proposals range from the ninth century to the fourth century BC, with many scholars favoring the Persian period. Among the Dead Sea Scrolls, as reported in the published editions, parts of Joel survive in the Qumran manuscripts of the Twelve Prophets (4QXII-c and others) and in the Wadi Murabbaʿat scroll of the Twelve (Mur 88); the Greek Minor Prophets Scroll from Nahal Hever (8HevXIIgr) is not reported to preserve Joel. These witnesses generally support the Masoretic Text. Verse numbers follow the standard English numbering. The Hebrew text divides the book into four chapters: English 2:28–32 is Hebrew 3:1–5, and English 3:1–21 is Hebrew 4:1–21.

verses.text: The word of Yahweh that came to Joel{a} son of Pethuel.

Hear this, you elders;
listen, all who dwell in the land!
Has anything like this happened in your days,
or in the days of your fathers?

Recount it to your children,
and let your children recount it to theirs,
and their children to the generation after.

Wake up, you drunkards, and weep;
wail, all you who drink wine,
over the sweet wine,
for it is snatched from your mouth.

For a nation has come up against my land,
mighty and past counting;
its teeth are a lion’s teeth,
and it has the fangs of a lioness.

Wail like a young woman{c} dressed in sackcloth
for the husband of her youth.

Grain offering and drink offering are cut off
from the house of Yahweh.
The priests mourn,
the ministers of Yahweh.

Gird on sackcloth and beat your breasts, you priests;
howl, you servants of the altar.
Come, lie all night in sackcloth,
you who serve my God!
For grain offering and drink offering
are kept back from your God’s house.

Set apart a fast;
call a solemn assembly.
Gather the elders
and all who live in the land
to the house of Yahweh your God,
and cry out to Yahweh.

Is not the food cut off
before our very eyes,
joy and gladness
from the house of our God?

To you, Yahweh, I call,
for fire has consumed
the pastures of the wilderness,
and flame has scorched
all the trees of the field.

Even the wild beasts pant for you,
for the streams of water have dried up,
and fire has consumed
the pastures of the wilderness.

notes.text: The name means “Yahweh is God.”

Four Hebrew words for locusts (gazam, ʾarbeh, yeleq, ḥasil), perhaps different species or stages of growth, perhaps simply poetic synonyms; the renderings here follow their probable root meanings. Compare 2:25.
Hebrew bethulah, often “virgin,” here probably a young bride whose husband has died before or soon after the marriage.
Hebrew tappuaḥ, perhaps the apricot or quince.
There is a wordplay in Hebrew: keshod mishshadday, “like destruction (shod) from Shaddai.” Compare Isaiah 13:6.
The Hebrew of this line contains three words found nowhere else, and its meaning is uncertain.
Or “bear the guilt.” The Septuagint reads “have perished.”

verses.text:
Blow the horn in Zion;
sound the alarm on my holy mountain!
Let all who live in the land tremble,
for the day of Yahweh is coming; it is near—

a day of darkness and deep gloom,
a day of cloud and heavy darkness!
Like the dawn spread upon the mountains
a people comes, vast and strong;
there has never been anything like it from ancient times,
nor will there be again after it
for years, from generation to generation.

Before it fire devours,
and behind it a flame blazes.
The land before it is like the garden of Eden,
and behind it a desolate wilderness;
nothing escapes it.

They look like horses,{a}
and they gallop like steeds of war.

With a noise like chariots
they leap on the mountaintops,
like the crackle of a flame of fire
consuming stubble,
like a mighty people
drawn up for battle.

Before them peoples writhe in anguish;
every face grows pale.{b}

None crowds his neighbor;
each goes in his own path.
Through the weapons{c} they burst
and do not break off.

The earth quakes before them;
the heavens shake.
Sun and moon grow dark,
and the stars withdraw their shining.

“Yet even now,” declares Yahweh,
“turn back to me with your whole heart,
with fasting, with weeping, and with mourning.”

Who knows whether he will turn and relent
and leave a blessing behind him,
a grain offering and a drink offering
for Yahweh your God?

gather the people.
Make the assembly holy;
bring together the elders;
gather the little ones,
even babies who nurse at the breast.
Let the bridegroom come out of his chamber,
and the bride from her canopy.

Between the porch and the altar{e}
let the priests who serve Yahweh weep
and say, “Have pity on your people, Yahweh,
and do not give your inheritance over to reproach,
for the nations to mock.
Why should they say among the peoples,
‘Where is their God?’ ”

Then Yahweh was zealous for his land
and had compassion on his people.

Yahweh answered and said to his people,
“Look, I am sending you
grain, new wine, and oil,
and you will be filled with them;
and I will no more make you
a reproach among the nations.

The northerner I will drive far from you,
banish him into a land dry and desolate,
his front ranks into the eastern sea,
his hindmost into the western sea.{f}
His stink will go up,
his reek will rise,
for he has done great things.

Be glad, children of Zion,
and rejoice in Yahweh your God,
for he has given you the early rain in righteousness;{g}
he has poured down showers for you,
the early and the latter rain, as before.

The threshing floors will be full of grain,
and the vats will overflow with new wine and oil.

I will repay you for the years
that the swarmer has eaten,
the hopper, the stripper, and the cutter,{h}
my great army, which I sent among you.

You will eat your fill and be satisfied,
and praise the name of Yahweh your God,
who has dealt wondrously with you.
And my people will never again be put to shame.

You will know that I am in the midst of Israel,
and that I am Yahweh your God, and there is no other.
And my people will never again be put to shame.

Even on male and female slaves
in those days I will pour out my Spirit.

I will show wonders in the heavens and on the earth:
blood and fire and columns of smoke.

The sun will be turned to darkness
and the moon to blood,
before the day of Yahweh comes,
the great and fearsome day.

And everyone who calls on the name of Yahweh
will be saved.{j}
For on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem
there will be those who escape,
as Yahweh has said,
and among the survivors
those whom Yahweh calls.”

notes.text: The head of a locust resembles that of a horse; compare Revelation 9:7–9. Whether chapter 2 describes a second locust plague, an invading army pictured as locusts, or the apocalyptic army of the day of Yahweh is debated.
Or “gathers a glow”; the Hebrew is uncertain (compare Nahum 2:10).
Or “through the water channels.”
Compare Exodus 34:6–7; Jonah 4:2.
That is, in the court of the priests, between the entrance porch of the temple and the altar of burnt offering.
The eastern sea is the Dead Sea; the western sea is the Mediterranean.

Or “the teacher of righteousness.” The Hebrew hammoreh can mean either “the early rain” or “the teacher”; the second sense was taken up at Qumran, whose leader was called “the Teacher of Righteousness.” The early rain falls in October–November; the latter rain in March–April.
See the note at 1:4.

Verses 28–32 are 3:1–5 in the Hebrew text. Peter quotes them at Pentecost (Acts 2:17–21), following the Septuagint with some changes (“in the last days,” and “my servants … my maidservants” in verse 29). Compare also Numbers 11:29.
Quoted in Romans 10:13, where Paul applies “the name of the Lord” to Jesus.

verses.text:
“For look, in those days and at that time,
when I restore the fortunes of Judah and Jerusalem,{a}

They cast lots for my people,
traded a boy for a prostitute,
and sold a girl for wine, and drank it.
“What are you to me, Tyre and Sidon, and all the regions of Philistia? Are you repaying me for something? If you are repaying me, swiftly and speedily I will turn your deeds back on your own heads.
For you took my silver and my gold and carried my rich treasures into your temples.{c}
The people of Judah and of Jerusalem you have sold off to the Greeks,{d} to remove them far from their own borders.
Look, I am going to rouse them from the place to which you sold them, and turn your deeds back on your own heads.
I will sell your sons and your daughters into the hand of the people of Judah, and they will sell them to the Sabeans,{e} to a nation far away; for Yahweh has spoken.”

Let the nations rouse themselves
and come up to the Valley of Jehoshaphat;
for there I will sit to judge
all the nations round about.

Put in the sickle,
for the harvest is ripe.
Come, tread,
for the winepress is full.
The vats overflow,
for their wickedness is great.{h}

Multitudes, multitudes
in the valley of decision!
For the day of Yahweh is near
in the valley of decision.

Sun and moon grow dark,
and the stars withdraw their shining.

Yahweh roars from Zion
and utters his voice from Jerusalem,
and the heavens and the earth shake.
But Yahweh is a refuge for his people,
a stronghold for the children of Israel.

“So you will know that I am Yahweh your God,
dwelling in Zion, my holy mountain.
Jerusalem will be holy,
and strangers will never again pass through it.

“On that day
the mountains will drip sweet wine,
and the hills will flow with milk,
and all the streambeds of Judah
will flow with water.
A fountain will come out from the house of Yahweh
and water the Valley of Shittim.{i}

Egypt will be made a desolation,
Edom a wasted wilderness,
because of the violence against Judah’s people,
whose innocent blood they shed in their land.

But Judah will be inhabited forever,
and Jerusalem from generation to generation.

notes.text: Chapter 3 is chapter 4 in the Hebrew text.

The name means “Yahweh judges” (compare “the valley of decision” in verse 14). Since at least the fourth century AD it has been identified with the Kidron Valley east of Jerusalem, but the name may be symbolic.
Or “palaces.”
Hebrew “the sons of the Yevanim,” the Ionians (compare Daniel 8:21).
The people of Sheba in southwest Arabia, traders on the incense routes.
Hebrew “Sanctify war,” since battle was begun with religious rites.
The reverse of Isaiah 2:4 and Micah 4:3.
Compare Revelation 14:14–20.
The name means “acacias.” Perhaps the dry wadi running from Jerusalem toward the Dead Sea (compare Ezekiel 47:1–12; Zechariah 14:8).
Or “I will declare innocent their blood that I had not declared innocent.” The Septuagint and Syriac read “I will avenge their blood and will not leave it unpunished.”
